network.overall_strategy: An element-conserving candidate network centered on the experimentally supported cyanoacetylene–HCN–ammonia chemistry, with electrical-discharge alternatives. Asparagine is represented correctly as HOOC–CH(NH2)–CH2–CONH2, without specified stereochemistry; these routes do not establish enantiopure L-asparagine. Exactly ten graph-distinct pathways are listed: six combinations of two nitrile-supply histories and three possible hydrolysis orderings, three precursor-supply variants of alanine/formamide contact-glow chemistry, and one direct spark-discharge product channel. These are not ten independently demonstrated synthesis mechanisms. Explicit hydrolysis intermediates expose the unresolved regioselectivity rather than assuming it. All stages use Surface settings, including atmospheric chemistry feeding surface collectors. Methane, nitrogen, ammonia, water, hydrogen, acetaldehyde and formamide are explicit supplied feedstocks; their delivery and concentration are boundary conditions, not unrepresented synthesis claims. Reaction nodes representing discharge mixtures are labeled observational macro-edges: their inventories admit elemental balance, but inferred H2 bookkeeping does not establish measured H2 evolution or a unique mechanism. Neutral molecular formulas provide atom bookkeeping; aqueous protonation equilibria are implicit. Proposed temperatures and pH windows are distinguished from reported conditions. Product accumulation requires cooler, locally UV-shielded water and limited hydrolysis exposure; no validated integrated geochemical operating window is claimed. Direct aspartate amidation is excluded because selective prebiotic activation is unestablished. The Bizzarri et al. (2026) irradiation result is not forced into this terrestrial network: its 243 K experiment and unresolved coproduct inventory do not justify a closed reaction under the specified surface conditions.

reactions.name: Reduced-gas discharge supply of HCN and cyanoacetylene: balanced macro-edge

conditions.temperature: Approximately 353 K water reservoir in the laboratory analogue; proposed collection at 300-310 K; discharge nonthermal
conditions.other: Electrical discharge through an anoxic CH4/NH3/H2-containing gas above water. Water vapor is a medium component, not a net reagent in this nitrile projection. Capture into bounded, initially alkaline surface water, approximately pH 9-10, is proposed; losses by volatilization, polymerization and Fe2+-cyanide complexation remain unquantified.

reactions.mechanism: Energetic fragmentation and radical recombination generate a mixture containing reactive nitriles. This node is a net source projection, not a concerted reaction or a fixed experimental HCN:cyanoacetylene product ratio. Hydrogen appears on both sides because it is initially supplied and also permits conservative net hydrogen bookkeeping.
reactions.reasoning: Reduced-gas discharge production of cyanoacetylene underlies Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966), as reviewed by Lemmon (1970). Jiang et al. (2014) provide a relevant reduced-gas discharge configuration, not a measurement of this particular joint nitrile inventory. The listed channel admits elemental balance, but assigning excess hydrogen to H2 is a stoichiometric model, not evidence of measured H2 evolution. Feedstock capture and concentration are proposed integrations, not demonstrated environmental yields.

reactions.name: Post-impact atmospheric photochemical HCN supply: net projection

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K proposed receiving surface waters; atmospheric photochemical layers have their own temperatures
conditions.pressure: Variable atmospheric pressure; receiving waters approximately 1 atm
conditions.other: Anoxic, transient reducing atmosphere with strong UV and energetic nitrogen activation. The modeled high-nitrile regime requires sufficiently methane-rich conditions, approximately CH4/CO2 greater than 0.1. This is an atmospheric feeder to the surface network, not aqueous N2 fixation.

reactions.mechanism: A multistep atmospheric radical network converts activated nitrogen and methane-derived carbon into HCN. The listed molecules give a conservative net projection; direct thermal reaction between methane and nitrogen is not implied.
reactions.reasoning: Wogan et al. (2023) model substantial HCN delivery following sufficiently reducing impacts. Their result supports atmospheric supply, not this equation as an elementary process or a universal Hadean atmosphere. Net H2 production is bookkeeping for the selected channel, not an extracted model yield. Continued nitrile delivery after cooling must be demonstrated; the network does not assume free HCN survives prolonged residence near 390 K.

reactions.name: Methane photochemical conversion to acetylene: net projection

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K receiving surface environment; atmospheric reactions are photochemically driven
conditions.other: UV-driven methane-rich atmospheric chemistry without molecular oxygen; acetylene is generated through a hydrocarbon radical network rather than low-temperature thermal cracking.

reactions.mechanism: Methane activation, carbon-carbon bond formation and successive dehydrogenation produce acetylene. Hydrogen recombination supplies the H2 term in this balanced net representation.
reactions.reasoning: Acetylene is a required precursor in the cyanoacetylene-forming atmospheric chemistry discussed by Wogan et al. (2023). This simplified methane-to-acetylene inventory is a proposed coarse-graining, not an independently measured yield or the full atmospheric mechanism. It is included because the following cyanoacetylene reaction actually requires acetylene.

reactions.name: Photochemical conversion of acetylene and HCN to cyanoacetylene

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K receiving surface waters; gas-phase reaction temperatures vary with altitude
conditions.other: Far-UV activation in atmospheric regions where suitable photons penetrate. Delivery of cyanoacetylene to cooler surface collectors follows gas-phase formation; no submerged far-UV chemistry is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: HCN photodissociation can supply CN and H radicals; CN adds to acetylene to form cyanoacetylene and another H atom. Hydrogen-atom recombination closes the displayed net inventory. Competing radical reactions are not represented by this individual channel.
reactions.reasoning: Wogan et al. (2023) explicitly include CN plus acetylene as a cyanoacetylene source. The full HCN-photolysis/recombination sequence used here is a conditional net channel, not a claim that all CN has this origin or that H atoms quantitatively form H2. Nitrile rainout and capture remain distinct environmental requirements.

reactions.name: Ammonia addition to cyanoacetylene

conditions.other: Concentrated anoxic surface water with proposed pH 8-9.5 and available free ammonia. These operating ranges are screening conditions, not a reproduced optimization from the historical study. Use locally shaded porewater after atmospheric collection.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of ammonia across the activated carbon-carbon triple bond gives an aminovinyl nitrile, represented without specifying E/Z geometry.
reactions.reasoning: This is the first proposed molecular step in the Asn-producing cyanoacetylene chemistry of Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966), summarized by Lemmon (1970). No mineral catalyst is required. Co-location of cyanoacetylene and free ammonia is essential; dilution, ammonia loss and competing oligomerization can suppress the channel.

reactions.name: HCN addition forming 2-aminosuccinonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed pH 8-9.5, allowing HCN/CN- and ammonia/ammonium coexistence. Concentration must be measured as free reactive species rather than total cyanide because reduced iron can sequester cyanide.

reactions.mechanism: Enamine-imine interconversion followed by cyanide addition and proton transfer gives NC–CH2–CH(NH2)–CN. The two nitriles subsequently have different positions relative to the amino group.
reactions.reasoning: Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970) support this aminodinitrile-centered explanation of Asn/Asp formation. The supplied findings do not establish a modern isolated-intermediate kinetic study or a unique elementary sequence. This step supplies the correct C4 skeleton without requiring direct amidation of aspartate.

reactions.name: Candidate hydration of the amino-adjacent nitrile
agents: Hydronium ions for general acid catalysis

conditions.other: Proposed acidic processing at pH 2-4 after the alkaline assembly stage. The environmental acidification step and useful residence time are not experimentally established for this network.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted addition of water to the nitrile directly attached to the amino-bearing carbon forms NH2CO–CH(NH2)–CH2–CN.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative microscopic branch within the experimentally supported overall partial-hydrolysis chemistry of Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970). Nitrile hydration is chemically conventional, but selective formation or accumulation of this particular monoamide is not demonstrated in the supplied findings. Hydronium has a specific catalytic role; no unsupported mineral selectivity is invoked.

reactions.name: Candidate alpha-amide hydrolysis to beta-cyanoalanine

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-3. Residence time must be determined from competing nitrile hydration and amide-hydrolysis rates; no selective yield or guaranteed geological operating window is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the amino-adjacent carboxamide releases ammonia in neutral-form bookkeeping and yields HOOC–CH(NH2)–CH2–CN.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative ordering of conventional hydrolysis steps. The overall Asn-forming partial hydrolysis is supported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970), but the supplied literature does not demonstrate beta-cyanoalanine accumulation in this sequence. Hydrolyzing this amide before hydrating the remaining nitrile may be kinetically disfavored; this is a competing candidate channel, not an established preferred route.

reactions.name: Candidate beta-cyanoalanine hydration to asparagine

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K proposed processing; 300-310 K proposed accumulation
conditions.other: Proposed pH 2-4 during hydration, followed by cooling and adjustment toward pH 5-7. Local UV shielding is required after formation. The time required to hydrate the nitrile without appreciable Asn loss is unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the side-chain nitrile creates CONH2 while retaining the existing alpha-carboxyl group, giving HOOC–CH(NH2)–CH2–CONH2.
reactions.reasoning: This is an atom-conserving, chemically conventional route to the correct Asn constitutional isomer, but its isolated abiotic implementation under these conditions is speculative in the supplied research. Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970) support the broader nitrile partial-hydrolysis family. Glavin et al. (2024) motivate limited heating and mild product recovery, not a quantified preservation guarantee.

reactions.name: Candidate hydration of the remaining nitrile to the diamide

conditions.other: Proposed pH 2-4. This competes with rxn_008; the graph does not assert that the two branches have comparable flux.

reactions.mechanism: The side-chain nitrile of NH2CO–CH(NH2)–CH2–CN hydrates to a second carboxamide, producing NH2CO–CH(NH2)–CH2–CONH2.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative intermediate-resolved branch of the partial-hydrolysis family supported at the overall level by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970). Including the diamide is chemically motivated because either nitrile can hydrate before an amide hydrolyzes; its accumulation and lifetime are not established by the supplied studies.

reactions.name: Candidate diamide hydrolysis at the amino-adjacent carboxamide

conditions.temperature: 320-350 K proposed processing; 300-310 K proposed collection
conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-3 processing followed by cooling and adjustment toward pH 5-7. Regioselectivity and residence time are unresolved; both monoacid regioisomers and further hydrolysis must be monitored.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis specifically of the carboxamide adjacent to the amino-bearing carbon gives the alpha-carboxyl group of Asn and releases ammonia. Hydrolysis of the other carboxamide would give a different constitutional isomer, not Asn.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative and a principal selectivity bottleneck. Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970) establish overall Asn-producing partial hydrolysis, not selective diamide hydrolysis as an isolated step. No catalyst-induced regioselectivity is claimed. Further side-chain amide hydrolysis can erase Asn, consistent with the preservation concerns discussed by Glavin et al. (2024).

reactions.name: Candidate hydration of the side-chain nitrile first

conditions.other: Proposed pH 2-4 after aminodinitrile assembly. This competes with rxn_007; no measured preference for either nitrile is available in the supplied findings.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the nitrile farther from the amino-bearing carbon gives NC–CH(NH2)–CH2–CONH2, retaining the amino-adjacent nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative microscopic alternative within the nitrile-hydrolysis framework of Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970). This branch has a chemical basis because the dinitrile contains two hydratable groups, but it is not an additional experimentally established Asn synthesis.

reactions.name: Candidate hydration of asparagine nitrile to the diamide

conditions.other: Proposed pH 2-4. Preservation of the already formed side-chain amide must compete successfully with further hydrolysis; no rate ratio is supplied by the literature.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration of the remaining amino-adjacent nitrile produces the diamide without changing the existing side-chain carboxamide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative ordering of standard nitrile hydration. Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970) support the overall precursor family but do not separately validate this intermediate sequence. This route converges chemically with rxn_010 rather than introducing an unrelated precursor solely for connectivity.

reactions.name: Reduced-gas discharge production of alanine: observational macro-edge

conditions.temperature: 353 K water reservoir in the laboratory analogue; proposed condensate collection at 300-310 K
conditions.other: Anoxic CH4/NH3/H2 gas-water discharge system, with a nonthermal spark region. Jiang-style runs used continuous discharge over days. Alanine must subsequently reach 100 mM for the modeled contact-glow step; that concentration is not established by the discharge experiment.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge chemistry produces carbonyls, nitrogen-containing intermediates and amino acids through an unresolved multireaction network. The listed inventory is a balanced projection of an alanine-producing channel, not a complete product mixture.
reactions.reasoning: Reduced-gas discharge amino-acid production is supported by Jiang et al. (2014). The exact allocation of methane, ammonia and water to alanine, and the corresponding net H2 bookkeeping, are not a measured elementary mechanism. Hydrogen is listed on both sides to retain the supplied hydrogen atmosphere while admitting net balance. Subsequent delivery to a concentrated contact-glow solution is a proposed integration, not an experimentally demonstrated continuous synthesis.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker formation of alanine nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed mildly alkaline water, approximately pH 8-9, with co-located acetaldehyde, ammonia and free cyanide. Use confined porewater to limit acetaldehyde and HCN loss; concentrations and competing oligomerization require measurement.

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde condenses with ammonia, releasing water; cyanide addition to the resulting imine or iminium species gives 2-aminopropanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is established Strecker chemistry (Strecker, 1850), rather than a newly proposed bond-forming reaction. Its integration into an Asn-producing prebiotic material history is speculative and is not demonstrated by the supplied Asn studies. Munegumi (2014) supports the downstream alanine/formamide experiment, not this specific upstream preparation or geochemical concentration history.

reactions.name: Alanine nitrile hydrolysis to alanine

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-3; nitrile hydrolysis proceeds through an amide. Cool and neutralize before contact-glow processing. Asparagine is not yet present during this warmer precursor treatment.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis give alanine and ammonia. The net reaction requires more than one water molecule; coefficients are intentionally not encoded in the input array.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis is the conventional completion of the Strecker synthesis (Strecker, 1850). Its specific connection to the concentrated Munegumi (2014) Asn experiment is speculative, not directly demonstrated in the supplied research. Alanine preparation can be spatially separated from Asn formation, avoiding the assumption that Asn survives the full precursor-hydrolysis treatment.

reactions.name: Alanine/formamide contact-glow production of asparagine: observational macro-edge

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K proposed controlled bulk liquid; exact reported bulk temperature unavailable in the supplied summary; plasma nonthermal
conditions.other: Reported feed concentrations: alanine 100 mM and formamide 200 mM. Contact glow discharge at an electrode-water boundary provides energy, not a mineral catalyst. An oxygen-free headspace is imposed for this network; anoxic replication and equivalence to natural lightning are not established by the supplied abstracts. Cool and locally shield collected products.

reactions.mechanism: Plasma-liquid radical chemistry produces an Asn-containing mixture. The displayed alanine plus formamide channel has a conservative net closure with H2, but a unique atom-mapped chain-extension mechanism and measured H2 coproduct have not been established.
reactions.reasoning: Munegumi, Shimoyama and Harada (1997) and Munegumi (2014) directly support Asn production; the latter reports 3.0% yield based on consumed alanine. That metric is not yield from all supplied carbon. The empirical product observation is stronger than the proposed closed net allocation: H2 is an accounting hypothesis, not a reported measurement. Concentrated feedstock co-availability, oxygen-free performance and natural plasma scaling remain unresolved.

reactions.name: Direct reduced-gas spark production of asparagine: observational macro-edge

conditions.temperature: 353 K reported water reservoir; spark region nonthermal; proposed product collection at 300-310 K
conditions.other: CH4/NH3/H2 and water, tungsten-electrode electrical discharge for three or seven days, with reported CH4 and NH3 replenishment. Electrodes supply electrical energy and are not assigned a catalytic role. The cooler collection temperature is a preservation proposal, not the reported reservoir temperature.

reactions.mechanism: An unresolved gas-liquid discharge network generates Asn among many products. The balanced inventory is a target-producing net projection; it does not identify which nitrile or carbonyl intermediates actually produced Asn. Initial hydrogen and conservative net hydrogen bookkeeping are represented by H2 on both sides.
reactions.reasoning: Jiang et al. (2014) directly detected Asn and reported high relative chromatographic abundance in the three-day mixture, but did not establish an absolute carbon yield or a unique mechanism. The H2 closure here is not measured H2 evolution, and the edge must not be interpreted as a complete experimental product balance. It may overlap mechanistically with the explicit nitrile pathways rather than constituting an independent elementary synthesis.

reactions.name: Competing asparagine side-chain deamidation to aspartic acid

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K; greater concern with prolonged warmer exposure
conditions.other: Background aqueous loss, accelerated by sufficiently acidic or alkaline conditions and increasing temperature. Proposed accumulation near 300-310 K and pH 5-7 reduces exposure severity but does not establish a safe lifetime. Molecular oxygen is unnecessary.

reactions.mechanism: Net hydrolysis of the side-chain carboxamide releases ammonia and gives aspartic acid. This free-molecule bookkeeping does not require assuming a peptide-specific succinimide mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Lemmon (1970) describes continued hydrolysis from Asn toward Asp, while Glavin et al. (2024) emphasize Asn loss during hot-water handling and the value of room-temperature extraction. This is a degradation sink, not a productive Asn route. The network includes no reverse Asp-to-Asn edge because selective prebiotic carboxylate activation and amidation have not been established.

pathways.name: Spark-fed nitrile route through beta-cyanoalanine
pathways.description: Discharge supplies HCN and cyanoacetylene; ammonia addition and cyanide incorporation build the aminodinitrile. The candidate ordering converts the amino-adjacent nitrile completely to a carboxyl group before hydrating the side-chain nitrile. The overall nitrile family is experimentally anchored, but this microscopic ordering is unvalidated.

pathways.name: Spark-fed nitrile route with amino-adjacent hydration followed by diamide formation
pathways.description: Uses the same supported nitrile-assembly family as P1, but both nitriles reach the amide state before the amino-adjacent amide hydrolyzes to the Asn carboxyl group. This is a distinct candidate hydrolysis ordering, not a separately demonstrated synthesis.

pathways.name: Spark-fed nitrile route with side-chain hydration first
pathways.description: The side-chain amide forms first, yielding asparagine nitrile; hydration of the other nitrile gives the diamide. Selective amino-adjacent amide hydrolysis would then yield Asn. The competing rates and regioselectivity are unresolved.

pathways.name: Photochemical atmospheric supply followed by beta-cyanoalanine formation
pathways.description: Methane/nitrogen photochemistry supplies HCN, methane photochemistry supplies acetylene, and a CN-mediated channel supplies cyanoacetylene. After surface collection, the candidate beta-cyanoalanine hydrolysis sequence produces Asn. Continued supply during cool conditions and capture efficiency remain open boundary conditions.

pathways.name: Photochemical atmospheric supply with amino-adjacent hydration and diamide convergence
pathways.description: Uses the atmospheric precursor history of P4 but follows amino-adjacent nitrile hydration, side-chain nitrile hydration and then the candidate Asn-forming diamide hydrolysis. Atmospheric support does not independently validate the aqueous microsequence.

pathways.name: Photochemical atmospheric supply with side-chain hydration first
pathways.description: Atmospheric HCN and cyanoacetylene feed aminodinitrile assembly, followed by the asparagine-nitrile and diamide ordering. This is a graph-distinct combination of a source history and a candidate microkinetic branch, not another independent experimental demonstration.

pathways.name: Direct Miller-type spark-discharge product channel
pathways.description: Simple reduced gases and water give an Asn-containing mixture in the Jiang experiment. This pathway has direct target-detection evidence but no resolved intermediate sequence, absolute Asn yield or experimentally closed product inventory. It may mechanistically include part of the nitrile family.

pathways.name: Spark-generated alanine followed by formamide contact-glow chemistry
pathways.description: Discharge-derived alanine is concentrated and combined with explicitly supplied formamide for contact-glow treatment. The two experimental modules are not an established continuous prebiotic synthesis; reaching the reported 100 mM alanine and 200 mM formamide concentrations is a required, unresolved integration condition.

pathways.name: Spark-HCN Strecker alanine followed by contact-glow chemistry
pathways.description: Spark-derived HCN reacts with supplied acetaldehyde and ammonia through conventional Strecker chemistry. Alanine is prepared, cooled and combined with supplied formamide before the empirical Asn-producing contact-glow stage. The full environmental material history remains unvalidated.

pathways.name: Photochemical-HCN Strecker alanine followed by contact-glow chemistry
pathways.description: Atmospheric HCN supplies the acetaldehyde Strecker branch, replacing the spark-derived HCN history in P9. The final contact-glow observation is experimentally supported, whereas precursor delivery, concentration and natural anoxic plasma integration are proposed rather than demonstrated.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically coherent realization of the experimentally supported cyanoacetylene/HCN/ammonia route described by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Lemmon (1970). However, aggregate Asn production does not establish this particular hydrolysis ordering. The principal uncertainty is rxn_008: the amino-adjacent amide must hydrolyze while the distal nitrile remains available for subsequent hydration, followed by preservation of the resulting side-chain amide.
suggestions: Measure time-resolved formation of mol_011, beta-cyanoalanine, asparagine and aspartate to establish the proposed ordering and competing reactions.
Specify pH, temperature, residence time and any hydrolysis catalyst; demonstrate an operating window that permits conversion without excessive rxn_019.
Attach reaction-specific references, distinguishing experimentally observed overall conversion from proposed individual hydrolysis steps.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Sequential nitrile hydration to the diamide is plausible, but neither its importance in the historical synthesis nor selective cleavage of its amino-adjacent carboxamide is established by the supplied evidence. Rxn_011 gives the correct target only with the stated positional selectivity; cleavage of the other carboxamide gives a different monoamide regioisomer. Explicitly identifying these steps as candidates is appropriate but does not resolve their kinetic uncertainty.
suggestions: Establish diamide formation experimentally and quantify cleavage at both carboxamides, including subsequent aspartate formation.
Retain the network's correct Asn connectivity. HOOC-CH2-CH(NH2)-CONH2, printed once as Asn in the supplied research synopsis, is the opposite monoamide regioisomer.
Demonstrate that conditions promoting rxn_011 do not destroy Asn faster than it accumulates.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The structural sequence is internally coherent, but preferential side-chain nitrile hydration in rxn_012 is not independently demonstrated. Subsequent diamide formation is chemically reasonable, while rxn_011 retains the same unresolved positional selectivity as P2. The supplied literature supports the broader nitrile-to-Asn conversion, not this specific sequence of isolated intermediates.
suggestions: Provide explicit structures or structural identifiers for mol_011 and mol_013 and distinguish them analytically; their identical formulas do not establish identical connectivity.
Measure competing hydration rates at the two nitriles rather than assuming side-chain-first processing.
Determine diamide hydrolysis branching and Asn survival under the same specified aqueous conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Wogan et al. (2023) support atmospheric production and delivery of nitriles in sufficiently reducing post-impact cases, but not these equations as elementary reactions. Rxn_004 needs interpretation as a photochemical net process involving CN radicals and hydrogen-atom termination. Delivery into cooler collectors is physically conceivable but unquantified, and the downstream route retains P1's unresolved hydrolysis ordering.
suggestions: Label rxn_004 explicitly as a net photochemical edge or expand it into HCN photolysis, CN addition to acetylene and hydrogen-atom termination.
Specify atmospheric composition, pressure and irradiation, and quantify rainout, losses, concentration and precursor survival during cooling.
Validate the beta-cyanoalanine hydrolysis sequence under the actual collector-water conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The atmospheric supply and aqueous diamide branches connect correctly. Nevertheless, Wogan et al. provide a conditional atmospheric source model, while Sanchez/Lemmon support aggregate Asn production rather than this diamide ordering. The unresolved requirements are retention of useful nitrile inventories during environmental cooling and preferential amino-adjacent carboxamide hydrolysis in rxn_011.
suggestions: Separate atmospheric photochemistry, collection and aqueous processing into condition-specific records without assuming a common temperature or irradiation regime.
Quantify whether delivered nitriles reach productive concentrations before volatilization, photolysis or competing aqueous reactions.
Measure diamide formation and positional hydrolysis selectivity together with the rxn_019 loss rate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid candidate graph, but its specific realization requires both side-chain-first nitrile hydration and selective diamide cleavage, neither established by the supplied studies. Atmospheric nitrile production is literature-supported only under particular reducing regimes. The Surface designation does not establish compatible irradiation, collection, hydrolysis and preservation conditions.
suggestions: Test whether mol_013 actually accumulates relative to the amino-adjacent hydration product.
Combine measured hydration and deamidation kinetics with a physically specified atmospheric-delivery and collector model.
Treat this as an alternative ordering within the experimentally supported nitrile route, not independent experimental confirmation of another mechanism.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Jiang et al. (2014) directly support Asn occurrence in reduced-gas discharge products, making this the strongest pathway for demonstrated target formation as represented. The observational macro-edge is appropriate and need not imply a resolved microscopic mechanism. Remaining limitations concern unspecified operating conditions, unmeasured branch stoichiometry and absolute yield, and the translation from sustained laboratory discharge to natural electrical activity.
suggestions: Record the reported 80 C water-reservoir temperature, discharge duration, gas replenishment and collection arrangement separately from proposed natural conditions; do not assign the reservoir temperature to the plasma.
Quantify absolute Asn production and destruction rather than interpreting chromatographic relative abundance as a synthesis yield.
Retain H2 as inferred bookkeeping unless its net production is measured, and specify the natural discharge and condensate-retention scenario.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Both discharge production of alanine and alanine/formamide contact-glow production of Asn have experimental support. Munegumi (2014) reports 3.0% Asn based on consumed alanine using 100 mM alanine and 200 mM formamide. What remains unestablished is whether spark-derived mixtures can supply a compatible concentrated feed and whether natural discharge reproduces the relevant engineered plasma-liquid conditions.
suggestions: Test contact-glow chemistry using characterized crude discharge-derived alanine mixtures instead of assuming compatibility with the purified-reagent experiment.
Provide a physical concentration and retention model consistent with the experimentally used solute concentrations.
Specify electrical operating parameters and distinguish demonstrated CGDE conditions from a proposed lightning analogue.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Acetaldehyde Strecker chemistry provides a sound route to alanine, and the final observational conversion is supported by Munegumi's contact-glow experiments. The unresolved integration issue is the composition, concentration and pH of the hydrolysate delivered to the discharge stage. Demonstrated alanine formation does not establish the required CGDE feed conditions or comparable Asn production in a crude mixture.
suggestions: Specify alanine-nitrile hydrolysis conditions and a physically justified transition to the contact-glow solution composition.
Measure residual cyanide, ammonia, salts and other products and test their effects on Asn production.
Demonstrate sufficient alanine accumulation and formamide co-location without assuming an unrepresented purification step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Strecker-to-alanine segment is chemically strong, and Asn formation from alanine/formamide is experimentally supported. This pathway additionally requires atmospheric HCN production and capture under a specified reducing regime. Its confidence is limited by unquantified HCN delivery and retention, hydrolysate compatibility, and the concentrated engineered contact-glow conditions, not by the number of stages.
suggestions: Connect a quantitative atmospheric HCN source and loss model to the acetaldehyde/ammonia collector rather than treating rxn_002 as an elementary reaction.
Specify hydrolysis, solution conditioning and concentration processes and test the resulting mixture in the Asn-forming discharge experiment.
Map Wogan et al. (2023), standard Strecker evidence and Munegumi (2014) to their respective edges without implying an experimentally demonstrated integrated sequence.

evaluation.network_feedback: The 20-molecule, 19-reaction network is connected, uses molecule IDs consistently and represents asparagine with the correct connectivity without claiming enantiopure L-Asn. Under the supplied deterministic check, all 19 reactions are conservation-valid: 13 are balanced as written and six are balanceable with coefficients. No conservation violations are assigned. Explicit coefficients should nevertheless be recorded, and observational macro-edge balance must not be interpreted as measured H2 evolution or resolved product stoichiometry. Literature alignment is strong for aggregate nitrile-route synthesis and for discharge-based Asn detection, but reaction-specific citations and numerical operating conditions are absent from the reaction records. The six nitrile pathways share experimental support for the overall conversion; their particular hydrolysis orderings and positional selectivities remain hypotheses. Rxn_019 is a chemically credible competing sink that must be included quantitatively when evaluating net accumulation. Surface is a plausible environmental umbrella, but atmospheric/plasma conditions, aqueous pH, temperature, concentration, residence time, transfer losses and product protection remain insufficiently specified. Declared feedstocks are legitimate boundary inputs, not missing synthesis steps; their delivery and co-concentration still require physical justification. P7 ranks highest because it has direct target-detection evidence, not because it has fewer steps. Overall confidence reflects the connected network's experimental anchors and unresolved selectivity, integration and survival constraints, not the number of pathways, hubs or environments. The network does not meet the 0.90 approval threshold.
